challenges.title: Architecture Review Board: the cache outage that took down the API
challenges.description: For 9 minutes on Thursday every CodeDev API call failed while PostgreSQL was healthy: Redis had stopped answering. Six statements on one evidence pack - the API dashboard (A), the dependency diagram (B), the timeout settings (C) and the review board's questions (D) - take you from reading the evidence to a hypothesis, past two wrong fixes, to the right fix and how to prove it.

questions.question:
Evidence A - API dashboard, Thursday 2026-10-22 (all 6 API instances):
time      req/s  5xx %  p95 ms   in-flight per instance (max 40)  Redis errors/s  PG CPU  PG p95
14:00     241    0.1      118     7                                0               34%     6 ms
14:02:30  236    38     30,002    40                               0               21%     5 ms
14:04     238    96     30,001    40                               8               11%     4 ms
14:08     240    97     30,001    40                               8               10%     4 ms
14:11:20  security group change rolled back
14:12     243    0.3      131     8                                0               35%     6 ms
(5xx at 14:04: 91% are 503 "server busy" returned at once by the in-flight limit, 9% are timeouts)

Evidence B - dependency diagram (as reviewed):
browser -> load balancer -> API (NestJS, 6 instances, 40 request slots each)
  every route except /health/live: AuthGuard -> SessionCache.get("session:<id>") -> Redis
                                   (no fallback; PostgreSQL has the sessions table but nothing reads it)
  GET /courses, /courses/:id, /lessons/:id: CatalogReader.get("course:<slug>") -> Redis -> on a miss PostgreSQL
  POST /lessons/:id/complete: AuthGuard, then progress service -> PostgreSQL (progress + outbox)
  GET /leaderboard: Redis sorted set (shows "unavailable" when Redis fails, lesson 9)
Redis: redis-main primary + 1 replica (Sentinel), both in subnet 10.20.8.0/24
Cause: at 14:02 a security group change dropped every packet from the API subnet to 10.20.8.0/24 (no reset, no error: connections just hang)

Evidence D - the review board's questions:
1. POST /lessons/:id/complete does not read the catalog. Why did it fail?
2. Would a second Redis replica have prevented this?
3. Should we run 12 API instances instead of 6?
4. What is the fix, what does it cost PostgreSQL, and how will you prove it before exam day?

Statement: "Board question 1: POST /lessons/:id/complete failed even though it does not read the catalog and PostgreSQL was healthy, because it waited on Redis too (AuthGuard's session lookup) and it competed for the same 40 request slots."
questions.explanation: True. B shows that every route except /health/live goes through AuthGuard, which reads the session from Redis with no fallback, so saving progress needed Redis as much as the catalog did. A shows the second path: in-flight requests at 40 of 40 on every instance, and 91% of the errors are instant 503s from the in-flight limit, so even a request that did not touch Redis could not get a slot. PostgreSQL's CPU and p95 went down during the incident because fewer requests reached it. The misconception is to look only at the routes that read the failing component: a shared resource (request slots) spreads a slow dependency to every route.

Evidence C - timeout settings (api/config/production.yaml):
redis:
  connectTimeoutMs: 30000
  commandTimeoutMs: 0           # 0 = wait for the reply forever
http:
  maxInFlightPerInstance: 40    # above that: 503 "server busy" at once
postgres:
  poolSize: 20                  # per instance
  statementTimeoutMs: 300

Statement: "The hypothesis that explains all of A: the API treated Redis as required and waited up to 30 s for it; 6 instances x 40 slots = 240 slots, and at about 240 requests/s each waiting 30 s, the slots were full within about a second, so the cache was a single point of failure for the whole API."
questions.explanation: True. C says a connection waits up to 30,000 ms and a command waits forever; B says the packets were dropped silently, so nothing failed fast. By Little's law, holding 240 requests/s for 30 s each would need about 7,200 concurrent requests, and the API had 240 slots: they fill in 240 / 240 = 1 s. That matches A: in-flight at 40 per instance, p95 30,001 ms for the requests that got a slot, instant 503s for the rest, Redis errors only once 30 s timeouts start to expire. It also explains the recovery at 14:12 as soon as packets flowed again. The misconception is to call this a Redis outage: Redis stayed healthy behind the dropped packets; the design turned a lost cache into a lost API.

3. Should we run 12 API instances instead of 6?

Statement: "Board question 2: yes. A second Redis replica with automatic failover would have kept the API up, so the read path can stay as it is."
questions.explanation: False. The replica that existed did not help, and a second one would not either: B says the security group change dropped packets from the API subnet to the whole Redis subnet, so primary and replicas were unreachable together, and Sentinel had no reason to fail over because Redis itself was healthy. Even when a failover does happen, it takes seconds to tens of seconds, and with 30 s waits the 240 slots fill in under a second. Replicas protect against one kind of failure (a dead Redis node); they do not change the fact that the read path cannot answer without the cache. The misconception is that redundancy of a component removes it as a single point of failure; the dependency is the problem, not the number of nodes.

Statement: "Board question 3: yes. With 12 instances (480 request slots) the API would have stayed up: the outage was a capacity problem."
questions.explanation: False. The slots did not run out because traffic was high: A shows about 240 requests/s, the same as before. They ran out because each request held a slot for 30 s. Doubling the slots to 480 moves the moment of exhaustion from about 1 s to about 2 s after Redis hangs, and then the API is down exactly as before, at twice the cost. More instances also open more connections that hang toward Redis. The misconception is to fix a latency problem (waiting too long on a dependency) with capacity; the cure is to stop waiting, with a short timeout and a fallback.

False. A dropped packet is not an error: redis.get only rejects when the 30 s connect timeout (or never, for commandTimeoutMs 0) expires, so every request would still hold a slot for 30 s before reaching the fallback, and the API would go down the same way. The fallback needs a short timeout of its own (50 ms, far above Redis's healthy p99 of about 1.2 ms), a circuit breaker so that, once Redis is clearly down, requests stop paying even those 50 ms, and single-flight per key so that a hot key does not send hundreds of identical queries to PostgreSQL's 20 connections. The misconception is that a try/catch makes a dependency optional: only a bound on how long you wait does.

questions.question:
Evidence D - the review board's questions:
1. POST /lessons/:id/complete does not read the catalog. Why did it fail?
2. Would a second Redis replica have prevented this?
3. Should we run 12 API instances instead of 6?
4. What is the fix, what does it cost PostgreSQL, and how will you prove it before exam day?

Verification plan in the review doc: "Chaos test in staging at exam-day load (340 submissions/s plus about 250 API reads/s): stop the Redis process for 10 minutes. Pass if read success stays >= 99.9%, p95 <= 300 ms and PostgreSQL connections stay below the pool size."

Statement: "This test alone does not prove the fix for Thursday's failure: a stopped Redis refuses connections within a millisecond, so the plan must also make Redis hang (drop its packets, as on Thursday) to exercise the 50 ms timeout."
questions.explanation: True. Stopping the process gives the client a connection refused error at once, which a plain try/catch already handles; it never tests the timeout, which is exactly what failed on Thursday. The chaos test must cover both modes: refuse (stop the process) and hang (drop packets with a firewall rule or a fault-injection proxy), and also the recovery (Redis back empty: the breaker closes, misses refill the cache, PostgreSQL load falls back). The pass criteria are good: they are the user-facing SLO (p95 300 ms for reads) plus the resource that would fail next (the PostgreSQL pool). The misconception is that any chaos test proves resilience; it proves only the failure mode it injects.

challenges.name: cache-single-point-of-failure
challenges.title: Single point of failure: the cache that took the API down
challenges.description:
On Thursday Redis stopped answering for 9 minutes and every CodeDev API call failed while PostgreSQL was healthy. Course pages and session lookups both read through CatalogReader.get, which treats Redis as required: when Redis refuses connections every request fails, and when Redis hangs every request waits for the client's 30 s timeout and then fails. When Redis is healthy, three learners opening the same new course at once send three identical queries to PostgreSQL. Fix CatalogReader.get so the cache is optional on the read path:
- Ask Redis with a 50 ms timeout: withTimeout(cache.get(key), CACHE_TIMEOUT_MS, clock). A value is a hit; null is a miss.
- A miss loads the value from PostgreSQL, then writes it back with cache.set(key, value) without waiting for the write (catch and ignore its failure), and returns the value.
- A Redis error or timeout loads from PostgreSQL instead (no write-back).
- Circuit breaker (already constructed: 3 consecutive failures open it for 1,000 ms): when breaker.allowRequest() is false, skip Redis and load from PostgreSQL. Call breaker.recordSuccess() when Redis answers (hit or miss) and breaker.recordFailure() when it errors or times out.
- Single flight: while a PostgreSQL load of a key is running, other loads of the same key wait for it instead of starting their own. Once it settles (value or error), the next load of that key goes to PostgreSQL again.
- An error from PostgreSQL (for example "not found: course:x") is the error of every request waiting for that load.
withTimeout and CircuitBreaker are existing helpers and are correct. Do not change them, the fakes or the test runner.

Input: { store, cache, events }: store is PostgreSQL (key -> value), cache the keys already in Redis, events in time order (ms on a fake clock): { at, request: key, id } calls reader.get(key); { at, redis: "up" | "down" | "hang", flushed? } changes Redis (flushed: it came back empty). Redis "up" answers in 2 ms, "down" refuses in 1 ms, "hang" never answers before the client's 30,000 ms timeout; PostgreSQL answers in 20 ms. At the same ms, Redis changes apply first, then due timers, then new requests.
Output (JSON): requests (each result with its latency), postgresLoads (loads per key) and peakConcurrentLoads.
hints: Follow one request through get() when Redis hangs: how long does it hold its request slot, and what does it return? Then do the same with 20 requests for one key arriving within a few milliseconds while Redis is down: how many PostgreSQL queries start?

Everything happens in get() and in one new private helper. Look at the first await (it has no time limit and no catch), at the await on cache.set (it puts a best-effort write on the response path), and at the direct store.load calls (nothing shares a load that is already running). The breaker exists but is never asked or told anything.

A similar fix for a feature-flag client: flags = await withTimeout(flagService.fetch(), 30, clock) inside try/catch; on error or timeout use the last known flags and call breaker.recordFailure(); skip the call while the breaker is open; and keep one in-flight fetch in a field (this.pending ??= fetch().finally(() => this.pending = null)) so that 100 concurrent requests make one call.
